solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Note is extensive, originally — reduce as much as possible

parts.note: a minim is a musical note, the half note

indicators.note: what a word is originally is how it starts: its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone contrasts a sprawling musical note with an instruction to cut everything down to the bone.
explanation.walkthrough: "Note" tempts you towards N or a letter-name like A to G, but here it is the whole word MINIM, the half note.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb means cutting a thing down to its smallest possible amount.

clue.text: Church service about death, on reflection, is insanity

indicators.note: a reflection shows a word back to front

parts.note: the Mass is a church service
END, death, written backwards; it sits inside MA…SS

explanation.surface: Someone declares that holding a service about death is sheer lunacy.
explanation.walkthrough: "Death" wants to be D, but D alone leaves the answer short; it is END, turned round and packed into MASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Madness and insanity are the same loss of reason.

clue.text: Relative in French city, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling may differ

parts.note: Nice, the city on the Riviera, is said 'neece'

explanation.surface: A family member is living in a French city, or so rumour has it.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice the French city is pronounced 'neece', not like the English word nice.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is a relative: your sibling's daughter.

clue.text: "I hate Smartphone," I snarled

indicators.note: a snarled line is tangled, so the letters are in a knot

explanation.surface: A grump barks out his loathing of the thing everyone else is glued to.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both jobs at once: the snarling hater is the misanthrope, and his words hold the letters. "Snarled" reads as a growl but works as tangled.
explanation.definitionFit: A misanthrope hates people and their ways; snarling at everyone's favourite gadget is exactly his style.

clue.text: Deprive celebrity very easily, to begin with

indicators.note: take only what the word begins with, its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it would be easy to take things away from a famous person.
explanation.walkthrough: "Deprive" is used in the sense of withholding what is needed, especially food.
explanation.definitionFit: To starve someone is to deprive them of food or of something they need.

clue.text: Professionals like to tour church

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go round it

parts.note: CE = Church of England; it sits inside A…S

explanation.surface: A group of professionals enjoys going round churches.
explanation.walkthrough: Aces are experts, the very best at something, which is how they stand for professionals.
explanation.definitionFit: Aces are highly skilled experts, close enough to professionals as opposed to amateurs.

clue.text: Insurrection after tea in horse-drawn carriage

parts.note: cha (or char) is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: An uprising breaks out after teatime inside a carriage pulled by horses.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA is informal British for tea, from the Chinese word; it turns up constantly in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A chariot is a two-wheeled carriage drawn by horses, as raced in ancient Rome.

clue.text: Extremely silly head movement in church court

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends

parts.note: a nod is a movement of the head

explanation.surface: Someone makes a ridiculous nod during a solemn church hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: "Extremely" looks like it intensifies silly; it means take the extremes of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A synod is an assembly of clergy that governs and rules on church matters.

clue.text: Doctor regularly reuses item of clothing

indicators.note: at regular intervals: every other letter

explanation.surface: A doctor keeps recycling the same bit of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: "Regularly" seems to describe how often the doctor reuses things; it picks out every second letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a frock is one particular garment, so the general 'item of clothing' points at it.

clue.text: Decline to vote? That's a black mark

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether sitting out a vote counts against you.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes the second half sound like a judgement on not voting; in fact it spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to decline to cast a vote either way.

clue.text: Defraud golf club for vodka and orange

parts.note: to screw someone is slang for cheating them
a driver is the golf club for long tee shots

explanation.surface: Someone swindles the golf club to pay for a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is also a tool, but here it is the cocktail of vodka and orange juice.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is the recipe: vodka topped up with orange juice is the cocktail sharing its name with the tool.

clue.text: Female sheep in tree, reportedly

indicators.note: as reported, spoken, so it is a sound

parts.note: the yew, an evergreen tree, is said 'you'

explanation.surface: Word has it that a sheep has got up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: "In" looks like it puts one thing inside another; it only links the definition to the sound. EWE and YEW are said identically.
explanation.definitionFit: The farming term: the female of the sheep, as ram is the male, is this word.

clue.text: New editor protects obnoxious people? Oh well

parts.note: ed = editor; N and ED go round the next piece

explanation.surface: A new editor shields some ghastly people, and someone shrugs about it.
explanation.walkthrough: "Oh well" is a resigned shrug, so the answer is an interjection, not a noun or verb. "Obnoxious people" is plural, which fits a collective word used of people as pests.
explanation.definitionFit: "Never mind" and "oh well" are both said when accepting a minor setback.

clue.text: Trifling insult

definitions.meaning: first definition: an adjective, small or minor
second definition: a noun, a snub

explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions are different parts of speech: an adjective meaning minor, and a noun meaning a snub.
explanation.definitionFit: Slight means trifling or small, and a slight is an insult or snub.

clue.text: I run over antelope in country

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means sits above

parts.note: the eland is a large African antelope

explanation.surface: A driver confesses to hitting an antelope somewhere abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: "Run over" reads as a traffic accident; it is really R placed over, above, the antelope in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the island republic west of Britain is one instance of a country.

clue.text: Change second character in Macbeth

parts.note: s = second, the unit of time
the three witches appear in Shakespeare's Macbeth

explanation.surface: A director recasts the second role in a production of Macbeth.
explanation.walkthrough: "Second character" wants to mean the second letter of Macbeth; "second" is S on its own and the character is a witch.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean swapping one thing for another, as in trading places.

clue.text: Rash vet disrupted the gathering of crops

indicators.note: things disrupted are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: An impetuous vet got in the way of the farm bringing in its crops.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rash" looks like a skin complaint a vet might treat; it simply describes the vet and gives letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictionary gloss: the noun names the season's work of bringing ripe crops in from the fields.

clue.text: Organised party with Mike without any definite plan

parts.note: to run an event is to organise it
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet, added on

explanation.surface: Someone throws a party with a friend called Mike, but nothing is really planned.
explanation.walkthrough: "Organised" sits oddly beside "without any definite plan", which hides that it just means RAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Random means happening without any definite plan or pattern.

clue.text: Engineer grouses at ancient browser

indicators.note: to engineer is to construct something, so the letters are rebuilt

explanation.surface: An engineer moans about a hopelessly out-of-date web browser.
explanation.walkthrough: "Browser" suggests internet software; here it is an animal that browses, feeding on plants.
explanation.definitionFit: The stegosaur was a plant-eating dinosaur, so literally an ancient browser of vegetation.

clue.text: Bemused anchorman hides chair

indicators.note: the phrase hides the answer inside itself

explanation.surface: A confused news presenter tucks a chair out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: A sedan, or sedan chair, is an enclosed seat carried on poles by two bearers.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan chair is a portable enclosed chair, so sedan alone can mean that chair.

clue.text: Save local court
Fake uniform found in toilets

parts.note: bog is British slang for a toilet
Uniform is U in the NATO alphabet; it sits inside BOG…S

explanation.surface: A counterfeit uniform turns up in the lavatories.
explanation.walkthrough: BOGS is everyday British slang for toilets.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something counterfeit, not genuine.

clue.text: Odd characters from Die Hard finish in cul-de-sac

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters: first, third, fifth, seventh

explanation.surface: Someone says a figure from the film Die Hard meets their end up a blind alley.
explanation.walkthrough: "Odd characters" pretends to be the film's eccentric cast; it means the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The French borrowing and the English phrase both name a street closed at one end with no way through.

clue.text: Start of vicious complaint is imprecise

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: ague, a fever with shivering, is an old word for an illness

explanation.surface: Someone says the start of a nasty illness is hard to pin down.
explanation.walkthrough: "Complaint" means an illness, not a grievance; AGUE is an old name for a malarial fever.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both adjectives describe something woolly and lacking exact detail.

clue.text: Bare necessities usually don't exist, at first

indicators.note: take each word at its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of Necessities Usually Don't Exist

explanation.surface: A remark that the bare necessities of life are, as a rule, not really there.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bare necessities" reads as one phrase; "Bare" is split off as the definition and the rest provides letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nude means bare, without clothes.

clue.text: Very sophisticated group examine male sheep from behind

indicators.note: read from behind, from the back, the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: A group of refined people inspect a ram from the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: TEST and RAMS join and the whole string is then read from the back.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase names the fashionable elite who set the tone in society.
